sources.title: Francis Ford Coppola (Q56094) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-15): English label 'Francis Ford Coppola', description 'American filmmaker (born 1939)', born 7 April 1939, no date of death, citizenship United States, Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Francis Ford Coppola' (article by Michael Barson, fact-checked by Britannica's editors; page updated August 2026) -- encyclopaedia biography: a director, writer and producer who had his greatest success and influence in the 1970s, 'when he attempted to create an alternative to the Hollywood system of film production and distribution'; covers the Warner Bros. split over his Zoetrope Productions, the Patton screenplay Oscar, The Godfather (a hit that the AFI ranked third on its 1998 list; Coppola nominated as director and sharing the adapted-screenplay Oscar with Mario Puzo), The Conversation, The Godfather Part II (Best Picture, Best Director and a shared screenplay Oscar), and Apocalypse Now (a $12 million budget that exceeded $30 million, a considerable part of the overrun paid by Coppola himself; 'generally regarded as a flawed masterpiece'; eight Oscar nominations). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (encyclopaedic assessment of his primary contribution; honouring but balanced in tone, so used for the achievement cards and orientation and never alone for a behavioural row). The page text breaks off after Apocalypse Now behind Britannica's subscription wall, so the 1980s-onward sections were not read, and the early-life passages and the page's AI-generated summaries were not used. Read as far as the page shows.

Princess of Asturias Foundation, 'Francis Ford Coppola', 2015 Princess of Asturias Award for the Arts, laureate page and jury minutes (Oviedo, 6 May 2015) -- the jury calls him 'an outstanding narrator' with a prominent place in film history, says his career 'has been a continuous struggle to maintain total independence as a creator and entrepreneur' as director, producer and screenwriter, and calls him essential for understanding the transformation and contradictions of the industry and art of filmmaking; the page's summary adds specialists' view of his 'genuine resolve to make auteur films within the confines of the major studios'. Award-body citation, honouring in tone; the foundation's biography tab did not load and was not read. Read the laureate page and the jury minutes in full.

Japan Art Association, Praemium Imperiale, 'Francis Ford Coppola' (25th laureate, Theatre/Film), profile, biography and chronology, 'a record of the laureate at the time of receiving the award' -- calls him one of the most influential directors, producers and screenwriters of all time; chronology and Oscar summary (the 1970 Patton screenplay Oscar; The Godfather, three Academy Awards; The Godfather Part II, six, including three for Coppola; The Conversation and Apocalypse Now, each a Palme d'Or); says he established American Zoetrope with George Lucas, 'a film company which encouraged young unknown artists to make personal and meaningful films'; and quotes him that for Apocalypse Now 'absolutely no one came forth to help me' and he went to the bank with all he had earned and the property he owned (self). Award-body profile, honouring in tone; its biography text is cut off behind a 'read more' control, so it was read as far as the page shows, and passages on his early life and his winery were not used.

Steve Pond, 'Honorary Oscars for Coppola, Wallach, Brownlow, Godard', TheWrap, 25 August 2010 -- trade-press report of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' announcement of its 2010 Governors Awards: the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award to Coppola, described as a 14-time nominee and five-time winner with Oscars for writing and directing the Best Picture winners The Godfather and The Godfather Part II and for writing Patton, honoured also for establishing American Zoetrope and backing films from The Black Stallion to The Good Shepherd; quotes the award's criterion (a producer 'whose body of work reflects a consistently high quality of motion picture production'). Press report of an institutional announcement; passages on the other honorees were not used. Read in full.

American Film Institute, AFI Catalog of Feature Films, 'The Godfather' (1972) -- catalogue entry whose History section is compiled from contemporary trade papers, newspapers and magazine features (Variety, Hollywood Reporter, New York Times, Los Angeles Times, Time) and from Coppola's DVD commentary: Paramount's option on Puzo's novel, the directors approached before Coppola, the casting history, Paramount's initial refusal to film in New York (Coppola prevailed before shooting began), real-location shooting, reported resistance from cinematographer Gordon Willis, the box-office and Academy Award results, and the continuity of Willis and designer Dean Tavoularis across all three films. Compiled institutional record that includes some of Coppola's own statements (self); passages on cast members and on other controversies were not used. Read the History notes in full.

American Film Institute, AFI Catalog of Feature Films, 'The Godfather Part II' (1974) -- catalogue entry compiled from contemporary trade press and magazine features: the decision to make the sequel as 'a true continuation', the continuity of Willis, Tavoularis, Puzo and the composers, Coppola taking over the producing duties, the film's final cut still unfinished weeks before release, his re-cutting of the last portion at his San Francisco Zoetrope facilities after a sneak preview and before the 12 December 1974 New York premiere, his insistence that the 200-minute film not be interrupted by an intermission, and its Academy Award results (six Oscars including Best Picture, Best Director and a shared Adapted Screenplay for Coppola). Compiled institutional record including Coppola's own quoted statements (self); passages on fees and cast negotiations were skimmed and not used. Read the History notes.

American Film Institute, AFI Catalog of Feature Films, 'The Conversation' (1974) -- catalogue entry compiled from trade press and the New Yorker: Coppola began the screenplay in 1966 and finished it in 1970, produced the film for The Directors Company that he formed with Peter Bogdanovich and William Friedkin, shot it in San Francisco including in his newly formed American Zoetrope studio (which the Catalog says made him one of the first major American filmmakers of his generation to open a studio outside Los Angeles), replaced cinematographer Haskell Wexler with Bill Butler after friction, left the footage with Walter Murch (whom a modern source quotes him calling 'an author' of the film), and the film's Palme d'Or and Academy Award nominations. Compiled institutional record; its closing news items were not used. Read the History notes in full.

American Film Institute, AFI Catalog of Feature Films, 'Apocalypse Now' (1979) -- catalogue entry compiled from contemporary trade press, the New York Times and magazine features, production notes held in the Academy's library and the 2001 Redux notes: development from John Milius's script bought for American Zoetrope in 1969, Coppola's 1975 decision to self-finance it as a $10 million independent feature, the casting and re-casting (including the replacement of an actor after four days of shooting), 238 days of filming from March 1976 to May 1977 interrupted by a typhoon, at least five release postponements, the 70mm run without screen credits and the Cannes 'work in progress' screening (a shared Palme d'Or), the choice of ending and the pulling of the 35mm prints, costs rising toward $31.5 million with Coppola putting up his estate as collateral, the divided critical reaction, and the 2001 Redux. Compiled institutional record that includes Coppola's own statements (self); passages on cast members' circumstances, on the political context of the location and on a published production diary were not used. Read the History notes in full.

American Film Institute, AFI Catalog of Feature Films, 'One from the Heart' (1982) -- catalogue entry (summary and notes completed with the AFI Academic Network) compiled from the New York Times, Los Angeles Times, Variety and other press: Coppola's refusal to direct it as a studio employee and his purchase of the rights for Zoetrope Studios, the move from romantic comedy to musical fantasy (about $8 million added), the withdrawal of foreign investors, the 'electronic cinema' press conference, his commitment of personal funds at $1 million a week, Paramount's veto of the release and his announcement ending Zoetrope's relationship with it, attempts to distribute the film himself, and the film's gross of under $10 million against about $25 million followed by Zoetrope's bankruptcy. Compiled institutional record including Coppola's own claims (self) and Paramount's contrary account; passages on a lender and on the later sale of the studio property were not used. Read the History notes in full.

Ian Freer, 'Walter Murch: A Conversation With The Legendary Sound Designer', Empire, 4 August 2017 -- interview with the editor and sound designer of The Conversation, the Godfather films and Apocalypse Now: Coppola's challenge to himself of combining Hermann Hesse and Hitchcock in The Conversation, his hiring Murch to edit it and leaving to prepare The Godfather Part II (returning about once a month for a screening), 'that's the way Francis works with everybody. He gives heads of department, and the actors, a lot of rope', and that none of Apocalypse Now's opening eight minutes was in the screenplay. First-hand collaborator's account some 40 years later, admiring but specific about process; passages on other films and on Murch's own projects were not used. Read in full.

Steve Hullfish, 'ART OF THE CUT with Walter Murch, ACE, on 7 of his films', ProVideo Coalition, 15 March 2020 -- editor-to-editor interview in which Murch describes how Coppola shot scenes in a documentary manner with several cameras and some improvisation (the Godfather wedding, The Conversation, the Apocalypse Now helicopter attack), his willingness to shoot 15 or 20 takes and his reasons, the deliberately artificial surveillance look of The Conversation, and the Godfather restaurant scene (Coppola and composer Nino Rota had designed an operatic moment, he held the music back until after the murder, and Murch added the elevated-train sound). First-hand collaborator's account, admiring but specific; passages on Murch's other films and on editing technique were skimmed and not used. Read the passages on the Coppola films in full.

April MacIntyre, 'Gordon Willis Interview', Below the Line (M&E), 1 July 2004 -- interview with the cinematographer of the first two Godfather films: Paramount 'wanted to make your standard gangster movie', Coppola 'saw it another way' and 'because he persevered, something great was fashioned'; the script, the use of Brando and Pacino, the framework of the film and Nino Rota's score were 'all Francis' while the visual structure was Willis's; Coppola re-hired him for Part II and again years later, and Willis says 'I'm not easy to deal with'. First-hand collaborator's account some 30 years later, with credit and criticism in the same answer; passages on other directors and on technique were not used. Read the passages on Coppola in full.

Gordon Willis, ASC, 'Interview at AFI' (Parts I and II), American Cinematographer, September and October 1978 (web pages posted February and March 2018) -- 1978 AFI seminar with the cinematographer: on the first Godfather he and Coppola were 'too busy fighting with Paramount to discuss anything'; on Part II their discussions were long and the relationship good; Coppola kept re-cutting up to the last minute, which forced the laboratory to make new matrices for each change; he laid out sequences in detail in advance; the one disagreement was over soft light; and the real changes came in the editing, cutting a six-hour film to three hours. Contemporary first-hand account. NOTE: theasc.com returned HTTP 403 to direct download, so these pages were read through the harness's web-extraction tool, which returns summaries and short excerpts; the claims used rest on short excerpts (the key passages were confirmed by a second extraction), only paraphrases are used, and no row relies on this source alone. Passages on the Lake Tahoe location and on technique were not used.

Stephen Pizzello, 'Apocalypse Now: A Clash of Cultures', American Cinematographer, February 2001 (web page dated 24 August 2017) -- roundtable interview with cinematographer Vittorio Storaro, joined by Stephen Burum, who supervised second-unit photography: Coppola gave Storaro 'the most freedom', described each day's main idea in metaphorical terms and left the technical means to him, said the responsibility for the film was his, supported the decision to flash the negative, and asked Burum 'What do you want to do?'. Collaborators' accounts of the 1976-77 production recalled in 2001. NOTE: theasc.com returned HTTP 403 to direct download, so this page was read through the harness's web-extraction tool, which returns summaries and short excerpts; only paraphrases are used and only as supporting evidence. Passages on photographic technique were not used.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'Premios Princesa de Asturias 2015 5.JPG' -- checked for the portrait's licence: photograph 'Own work' by Ruben Ortega taken on 23 October 2015 at the Princess of Asturias Awards ceremony in Oviedo (structured data depicts Francis Ford Coppola), published by the copyright holder under CC BY-SA 4.0 with the requested credit 'Rubén Ortega; CC-BY-SA'; the original's EXIF names the photographer as author and copyright holder; no restriction template. Not used for any scoring.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_coppola_afi_apocalypse, src_coppola_afi_oneheart, src_coppola_britannica, src_coppola_praemium | 1975-1982 | film-archive catalogue built from contemporary trade press and newspapers + encyclopaedia + award-body profile] The AFI Catalog records that in 1975 he decided to self-finance Apocalypse Now as a $10 million independent feature through his own new company and that, as costs climbed toward $31.5 million, he used his estate as collateral for a loan to cover the overage (his stake is given as $16 million in one report and $22 million in his own claim); Britannica likewise says the budget grew from $12 million to over $30 million with a considerable part of the overrun paid by Coppola himself, and the Praemium Imperiale profile quotes him that he went to the bank with all he had earned and the property he owned (self). For One from the Heart (1981) the AFI Catalog says he turned a romantic comedy into a musical fantasy that added about $8 million, committed $1 million a week of his own money after foreign investors withdrew, and pledged $1 million of his property as collateral for a bank loan, and that Zoetrope went bankrupt after the film grossed under $10 million on a cost of about $25 million. Two large, separate, independently reported decisions to stake his own assets, the second ending in a loss, so documented at a high confidence but below the extreme band because the evidence is concentrated in two projects and rests partly on his own statements. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest rows rest on a film-archive catalogue compiled from trade press and on award-body citations, with the editor and cinematographer accounts mostly admiring; score and confidence lowered.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_coppola_asturias, src_coppola_britannica, src_coppola_praemium, src_coppola_afi_conversation, src_coppola_afi_oneheart, src_coppola_afi_godfather | 1969-2015 | award-body citations + encyclopaedia + film-archive catalogue built from trade press] The Princess of Asturias jury calls his career 'a continuous struggle to maintain total independence as a creator and entrepreneur', Britannica says that in the 1970s he tried to create an alternative to the Hollywood system of production and distribution, and the Praemium Imperiale profile says he established American Zoetrope with George Lucas; the AFI Catalog adds that he formed The Directors Company with Peter Bogdanovich and William Friedkin and shot The Conversation in his own San Francisco studio, which it says made him one of the first major American filmmakers of his generation to open a studio outside Los Angeles, that he resisted working as a studio employee on One from the Heart and bought its rights for Zoetrope instead, that in 1982 talks with two distributors failed over his demands for a lower distribution fee, an advance and retention of the film's other rights, and that during The Godfather he was angry about Paramount's initial refusal to film in New York and prevailed before shooting began. Independent archive and encyclopaedia accounts agree with the award bodies across five decades, though the citations are honouring, so documented at a moderate-high confidence. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest rows rest on a film-archive catalogue compiled from trade press and on award-body citations, with the editor and cinematographer accounts mostly admiring; score and confidence lowered.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_coppola_afi_godfather, src_coppola_afi_conversation, src_coppola_afi_apocalypse, src_coppola_afi_oneheart, src_coppola_willis_btl, src_coppola_willis_asc | 1970-2004 | film-archive catalogue built from trade press + cinematographer interviews] The AFI Catalog reports from contemporary news items that Coppola was angry at Paramount's initial refusal to film The Godfather in New York and prevailed, that Haskell Wexler was replaced as cinematographer on The Conversation within weeks after friction with the director, that at Cannes in 1979 he criticised Daily Variety for reviewing Apocalypse Now after critics had agreed not to review a work in progress, and that in January 1982, after Paramount vetoed the release of One from the Heart, he held previews at Radio City Music Hall that Paramount had not authorised and announced the end of Zoetrope's relationship with the studio (Paramount in turn cited his shooting schedule and the previews as breaches); cinematographer Gordon Willis told American Cinematographer in 1978 that on the first Godfather he and Coppola were too busy fighting with Paramount to discuss anything, and says in 2004 that Paramount wanted a standard gangster picture and Coppola persevered. A repeated willingness to confront studios, critics and collaborators is documented by an independent compilation and a collaborator, and the same pattern ended his studio partnership with Paramount, hence dual-edged at a moderate confidence.

persistence.rationale: [src_coppola_willis_btl, src_coppola_afi_conversation, src_coppola_afi_apocalypse, src_coppola_afi_godfather2, src_coppola_willis_asc | 1966-2004 | cinematographer interviews + film-archive catalogue built from trade press] Willis says that Paramount wanted a standard gangster movie and that 'because he persevered, something great was fashioned'; the AFI Catalog records, from a 1974 New Yorker article, that Coppola began the screenplay for The Conversation in 1966 and finished it in 1970, that principal photography of Apocalypse Now lasted 238 days after a typhoon ruined many of the sets and its release was postponed at least five times in 1977-78, and that for The Godfather Part II he was still re-cutting weeks before the December 1974 premiere and re-cut the film's last portion after a sneak preview showed it losing the audience; Willis adds in 1978 that he kept re-cutting up to the very last minute. Several independent descriptions of sustained effort over years, with admiring and critical accounts of its costs, so documented at a moderate confidence.

experimentation.rationale: [src_coppola_murch_pvc, src_coppola_murch_empire, src_coppola_afi_oneheart, src_coppola_afi_apocalypse, src_coppola_afi_conversation | 1972-2020 | editor's interviews + film-archive catalogue built from trade press] Murch says Coppola shot scenes such as the Godfather wedding, the opening of The Conversation and the Apocalypse Now helicopter attack in a documentary manner, launching actors into a scene, sometimes allowing improvisation, and covering it with several cameras, and that in The Conversation and other films he would let takes run to 15 or 20 so that actors who had gone past the obvious might produce 'something unique'; he also wanted an unsettling surveillance-camera look, with deliberately robotic pans, and set himself the challenge of combining Hermann Hesse and Hitchcock; the AFI Catalog records that for One from the Heart he announced 'electronic cinema' at a press conference, shooting scenes on videotape first and editing them before committing the final cut to film, that Apocalypse Now was first shown in 70mm without screen credits and was reassembled from the raw dailies in 2001 as a 196-minute Redux, and that The Conversation was shot in his own San Francisco studio. Repeated method experiments across three decades are documented by an editor and an archive, with mixed results (the electronic-cinema film failed), so documented at a moderate-high confidence. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest rows rest on a film-archive catalogue compiled from trade press and on award-body citations, with the editor and cinematographer accounts mostly admiring; score and confidence lowered.

collaboration.rationale: [src_coppola_murch_empire, src_coppola_willis_btl, src_coppola_storaro_asc, src_coppola_afi_conversation, src_coppola_afi_godfather, src_coppola_willis_asc | 1972-2004 | editor's and cinematographers' interviews + film-archive catalogue] Murch says Coppola 'gives heads of department, and the actors, a lot of rope', and that when he hired him to edit The Conversation he said he would leave after shooting to prepare The Godfather Part II and return about once a month for a screening; the AFI Catalog adds that a later source quotes Coppola calling Murch 'an author' of the film and that Willis and production designer Dean Tavoularis worked on all three Godfather films; Willis says Coppola re-hired him for Part II and again years later and that the script, the idea of using Brando and Pacino, the framework of the film and Nino Rota's score were 'all Francis' while he describes himself as 'not easy to deal with'; Storaro, in a 2001 American Cinematographer roundtable, called Coppola the director who gave him the most freedom, and Stephen Burum recalled him asking 'What do you want to do?' (both from page excerpts). The same sources record friction (Haskell Wexler's replacement on The Conversation, reported resistance from Willis on the first Godfather), so the picture is of wide delegation to repeat collaborators with real conflict, documented by four independent collaborators at a moderate-high confidence.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_coppola_praemium, src_coppola_wrap, src_coppola_afi_conversation, src_coppola_asturias, src_coppola_britannica | 1969-2015 | award-body profiles + press report of the Academy's announcement + film-archive catalogue + encyclopaedia] The Praemium Imperiale profile says that in 1969 he established American Zoetrope with George Lucas to encourage young unknown artists to make personal films; TheWrap's report of the Academy's 2010 announcement says the Thalberg Award honoured his establishment of American Zoetrope and his backing of films from The Black Stallion to The Good Shepherd; the AFI Catalog adds that he formed The Directors Company with Peter Bogdanovich and William Friedkin and opened a San Francisco studio; Britannica says he tried to create an alternative to the Hollywood system of production and distribution, and the Asturias jury calls him a creator and entrepreneur. Repeated self-started institutions and a record of backing other directors' films are documented by two award bodies, the press and an archive, but the descriptions are honouring and concern outcomes more than day-to-day behaviour, so documented at a moderate confidence. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest rows rest on a film-archive catalogue compiled from trade press and on award-body citations, with the editor and cinematographer accounts mostly admiring; score and confidence lowered.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_coppola_willis_asc, src_coppola_murch_pvc, src_coppola_afi_godfather2, src_coppola_afi_apocalypse | 1974-2020 | cinematographer interview + editor's interview + film-archive catalogue] Willis told American Cinematographer in 1978 that Coppola kept re-cutting The Godfather Part II right up to the last minute, forcing the laboratory to make new matrices for each change (from a page excerpt); Murch says he sometimes shot 15 or 20 takes; the AFI Catalog adds that after a sneak preview he re-cut the film's last portion before the premiere, that he pulled the 35mm prints of Apocalypse Now and re-circulated them with the credits over black after concluding that the explosions over the credits suggested a militant theme, and that in 2001 he reassembled the film from the dailies as Redux. Several independent accounts of repeated reworking, with real costs to collaborators, but they describe revision rather than any stated standard, so strong inference at a modest confidence.

ambiguity_tolerance.rationale: [src_coppola_murch_pvc, src_coppola_murch_empire, src_coppola_afi_apocalypse, src_coppola_willis_asc | 1972-2020 | editor's interviews + film-archive catalogue + cinematographer interview] Murch says that when Coppola covers a scene with several cameras he has to 'intuit' what happened and decides after each take whether to repeat it or move the cameras, aiming for 'serendipitous moments', and that none of Apocalypse Now's opening eight minutes was in the screenplay but emerged during editing; the AFI Catalog records that Apocalypse Now's release was postponed at least five times, that trial screenings ran from 139 to 165 minutes while the press speculated about alternate endings, and that he first showed it at Cannes as a work in progress; Willis says in 1978 that the real changes to Part II came in the editing, when a six-hour cut was reduced to three hours (from a page excerpt). Independent accounts show him working without a fixed endpoint and letting the film take shape in the cutting room, but they describe method and outcomes rather than his stated attitude to uncertainty, so strong inference at a modest confidence.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-15) for Q56094 returned en label 'Francis Ford Coppola', description 'American filmmaker (born 1939)', born 1939-04-07, no death date, citizenship United States (Q30), ko label present; the lead's hint was correct. SLUG/QID CHECK: no existing production or candidate file for slug francis-ford-coppola or QID Q56094 in the roster50 worktree (the only repository mentions of his name are inside other people's text). Region north_america is a valid controlled value; occupationId film_director, fieldId film, archetypes creative_creator and independent_creator, tags founder, innovator and independent, and impact domains artistic, cultural and innovation are existing vocabulary ids used by other candidates (film_director and film as for Scorsese, Spielberg and Kubrick). ZERO POLITICS: no political material is scored (the Apocalypse Now location arrangements with a foreign government, the film's war politics, and honours presented at government events are unscored). LIVING SUBJECT: only documented public professional behaviour is scored (productions, studio and financing decisions, working methods as described by collaborators and film archives). Excluded: family and family business (relatives who worked on his films, his wife's production diary, family-run companies), private life, health (his own and cast members'), the winery business, coverage of Megalopolis, any allegation, lawsuit or dispute with a lender or camera operator, reports of strain on him during The Godfather, personal wealth beyond the documented financing decisions, and any inferred motive or psychology; the AFI Godfather entry contains a passage on a reported strain during production, which was read and not used. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Francis Ford Coppola' (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Francis-Ford-Coppola), read to the point where the page breaks off behind its subscription wall (after Apocalypse Now): it says he enjoyed his greatest success and influence in the 1970s when he attempted to create an alternative to the Hollywood system of film production and distribution; supported by the Princess of Asturias jury citation, the Praemium Imperiale profile and TheWrap's report of the Academy's Thalberg Award (all honouring in tone, so used for the achievement cards and orientation only). READ (15 cited non-Wikidata sources plus the Commons page): Britannica; the Princess of Asturias Foundation laureate page and jury minutes; the Praemium Imperiale profile; TheWrap on the 2010 Thalberg Award; the AFI Catalog History notes for The Godfather, The Godfather Part II (the cast-negotiation passages skimmed), The Conversation, Apocalypse Now and One from the Heart; Walter Murch in Empire (2017) and in ProVideo Coalition (2020; the passages on the Coppola films read in full); Gordon Willis in Below the Line (2004); Gordon Willis's 1978 AFI interview and the 2001 Storaro roundtable in American Cinematographer (these two read only through the harness's page-extraction tool because theasc.com blocks direct download: short excerpts and summaries, used as supporting evidence only, with the key passages confirmed by a second extraction). Read but not cited: the No Film School piece on Zoetrope (a blog summary of a video essay), Slashfilm's retelling of Coppola's own Deadline remarks on being nearly fired from The Godfather (self, and about job security), Den of Geek's interview with author Mark Seal about his Godfather book (secondary; it also covers organised-crime pressure and a reported attempt at a crew coup, none of which was used), the Library of Congress item and rights pages for a 1973 Bernard Gotfryd photograph, and Wikimedia Commons categories. PERSPECTIVES: the editor and sound designer (Murch); two cinematographers (Willis, Storaro) and a second-unit cinematographer (Burum); a film-archive catalogue compiling contemporary trade-press and newspaper reports (Variety, Hollywood Reporter, New York Times, Los Angeles Times, Time, the New Yorker), which also records Paramount's contrary account and critics' views; two award bodies; the Academy's announcement as reported by the press; an encyclopaedia; and Coppola's own statements as quoted in the AFI entries and the Praemium Imperiale profile (self; never sole support for a row). CALIBRATION: the behavioural evidence is strong and comes from several independent collaborators and a compiled archive, but the collaborator accounts are admiring in tone, the award citations honour him, the archive passes on some of his own claims, and the best-documented episodes concentrate in Apocalypse Now and One from the Heart, so no score exceeds 82 and no confidence exceeds 0.70; the AFI entries do record failures, Paramount's contrary claims and hostile reviews, and Willis supplies a candid critical voice. Traits NOT scored: decisiveness (isolated decisions such as replacing an actor after four days, no pattern source), belief updating (the 35mm-prints reversal and the Part II re-cut rest partly on his own account), planning orientation (documented detailed pre-planning of sequences and a screenplay gestated from 1966, but the improvisation evidence cuts the other way), creative originality (overlaps the experimentation row and rests on critics' praise), persuasiveness (the Brando screen-test story is told as legend in one secondary retelling), leadership drive and impact motivation (no two independent episodes). DATE AND FACT CONFLICTS RECORDED: the AFI Part II entry dates a sneak-preview report inconsistently (a Time issue of 13 November reporting a 27 November preview), so no preview date is used; Apocalypse Now's financial obligation is $16 million in one report and $22 million in his own claim (the rationale states both); Britannica says the Patton Oscar was shared with a person the other sources do not name as the co-writer, so no co-writer is named; Britannica puts the Apocalypse Now cost at over $30 million and the AFI Catalog at $31.5 million, so the cards avoid a total and the moment attributes $31.5 million to the AFI Catalog.
